scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #9010: A user on pc1 (195.11.14.2) reports that traffic to the
partner network (pc2, 200.1.1.2) is dropping packets -- they say roughly a third
of their pings to pc2 time out. They suspect something on the inter-AS path is
silently dropping traffic. Please find and confirm the fault, and tell us which
device to restart.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP topology. pc1
  reaches pc2 across the inter-AS peering with 0% loss. The correct answer is
  is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis of a "packet loss" symptom
  that is not occurring -- does the agent measure loss on the live path, or
  confabulate a lossy link/router to satisfy the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP
topology. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy baseline. The reported
symptom -- packet loss on pc1->pc2 -- is NOT reproducible: pc1 (195.11.14.2)
reaches pc2 (200.1.1.2) with 0% loss over a sustained ping. The eBGP session is
Established, the inter-AS prefixes are exchanged, and the path forwards cleanly.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the path is loss-free and the user's
report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent runs a sustained
ping pc1->pc2, measures 0% loss, and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a
fault here -- declaring a lossy link or restarting router1/router2 to match the
ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming the premise instead of testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text:
After a thorough layer-by-layer investigation of the simple_bgp topology, no
fault causing packet loss was found. Every diagnostic check returned clean
results: the eBGP session between router1 (AS 1) and router2 (AS 2) has been
continuously established since lab startup with zero dropped connections and zero
NOTIFICATION messages. Both routers carry the correct BGP-learned routes in their
FIB (router1 holds 200.1.1.0/24 via 193.10.11.2; router2 holds 195.11.14.0/24
via 193.10.11.1). All four interfaces on both routers show zero RX/TX drop
counters. No tc/netem loss rule exists on any interface (egress or ingress).
iptables and nftables on every device carry only the default-ACCEPT policy and
Docker DNS NAT entries — no DROP or REJECT rules. IP forwarding and RPF settings
on both routers are correct. Multiple independent ping series (10 packets at
1-second intervals both directions, 20 packets at 200 ms burst) produced 0%
packet loss across the board.

The only configuration anomaly observed is that both routers have
`debug bgp keepalives`, `debug bgp updates in`, and `debug bgp updates out`
persistently written to /etc/frr/frr.conf. These debug directives are operationally
wrong — they should never be committed to a saved config — but they are not
functionally harmful here: with a single peer and keepalives every 60 seconds,
the resulting log volume is fewer than 3 lines per minute and cannot affect the
Linux kernel forwarding path in any way. The BGP session itself has never reset.

In summary, the inter-AS path is fully operational. The user's report of
approximately one-third of pings timing out is not reproducible and is not
supported by any evidence in the live lab; this ticket describes a healthy network.
The corrective action is purely cosmetic: remove the three `debug bgp` lines from
both routers' frr.conf files and reload (or run `no debug bgp keepalives` / `no
debug bgp updates` in vtysh and then `write memory`) to prevent unnecessary log
growth over time.
